working_theory_updates.claim: Crossing the alpha=0.10 order-statistic boundary from 18 to 19 personal examples is by itself a safe calibration-readiness jump.
working_theory_updates.interpretation: The second-largest-score threshold produced substantially fewer full-label sets, but the worst-subject coverage cost exceeded the preregistered safety bound. More personal calibration can cross a discrete informativeness boundary without guaranteeing subgroup-safe coverage.

working_theory_updates.claim: Subject baseline mismatch is a material source of poor wearable-state representation.
working_theory_updates.interpretation: Per-subject robust normalization improved classifier accuracy by 15.85 percentage points, roughly halved full-label sets, and retained mean coverage near the 0.90 target. This supports separating stable subject baselines from within-subject state changes before calibration.

working_theory_updates.claim: Subject normalization uniformly repairs the two post-selected difficult subjects S2 and S4.
working_theory_updates.interpretation: Normalization almost solved S4 under this split design but made S2 substantially more ambiguous. A population-level representation repair can hide subject-specific failure modes, so readiness must remain subject-conditional.

working_theory_updates.claim: A single sensor family can interfere with subject-level state discrimination.
working_theory_updates.interpretation: Removing temperature features was the only preregistered single-family ablation to pass. This diagnoses predictive interference in this representation; it does not establish temperature sensor malfunction or a general recommendation to discard temperature.

working_theory_updates.claim: Replacing shared-covariance LDA with either fixed diagonal QDA or distance-weighted k-nearest neighbors repairs the difficult subjects.
working_theory_updates.interpretation: The two fixed nonlinear alternatives either sacrificed cohort accuracy or increased ambiguity. Complexity alone is not a representation repair.

revised_j_jump_candidate.name: Subject-conditional calibration readiness surface
revised_j_jump_candidate.statement: The useful transition is not a single jump in calibration count. Readiness lies on at least two coupled axes: threshold stability from enough representative calibration examples, and representation adequacy after removing subject baselines or interfering signals. Crossing one axis can expose failure on the other.
revised_j_jump_candidate.next_falsification: Pre-register a nested held-out-subject study that crosses raw versus subject-normalized representations with calibration counts above and below the order-statistic boundary, then tests whether the apparent S4 repair and S2 failure replicate across temporal blocks and sessions without post-selecting subjects.

guardrails: S2 and S4 were post-selected after Experiment 9 and remain exploratory.
The k=18 to k=19 comparison tests one discrete order-statistic boundary, not all calibration-size effects.
Temperature ablation identifies predictive interference, not hardware failure or physiological irrelevance.
The nonlinear model comparison is limited to two fixed untuned NumPy implementations.
One WESAD session per subject prevents a direct test of cross-session stability.
No literature novelty claim has been made.
